225| \begin{definition}[Resolutions]\label{def:b3:asymmetric-synthesis:resolution}
226| The \emph{resolution of a racemate}\index{resolution of a racemate} is its
227| separation into enantiomers, classically by crystallising diastereomeric salts
228| with an enantiopure acid or base. In a \emph{kinetic resolution}\index{kinetic resolution}
229| the two enantiomers react at different rates with a chiral reagent or
230| catalyst, with selectivity $s = k_{\mathrm{fast}}/k_{\mathrm{slow}}$. In a \emph{dynamic kinetic
231| resolution}\index{dynamic kinetic resolution} the substrate enantiomers
232| interconvert fast while one of them reacts.
233| \end{definition}
234| 
235| \begin{theorem}[Kagan equation]\label{thm:b3:asymmetric-synthesis:kagan}
236| In a kinetic resolution of a racemate by first-order reactions of selectivity $s$,
237| the conversion $c$ and the ee of the remaining substrate are related by
238| \[
239|   s = \frac{\ln[(1 - c)(1 - \mathrm{ee})]}{\ln[(1 - c)(1 + \mathrm{ee})]}.
240| \]
241| \end{theorem}
242| 
243| \begin{proof}
244| Each enantiomer decays exponentially: the fractions left are $f_1 = \eu^{-k_{\mathrm{fast}}t}$ and
245| $f_2 = \eu^{-k_{\mathrm{slow}}t}$, so $\ln f_1 = s\ln f_2$. Starting from equal amounts, $1 - c = (f_1 + f_2)/2$ and
246| $\mathrm{ee} = (f_2 - f_1)/(f_1 + f_2)$. Then $(1 - c)(1 - \mathrm{ee}) = \tfrac12(f_1 + f_2)\cdot 2f_1/(f_1 + f_2) = f_1$ and likewise
247| $(1 - c)(1 + \mathrm{ee}) = f_2$. Hence $s = \ln f_1/\ln f_2$ is the stated ratio.
248| \end{proof}

271| \begin{proposition}[Dynamic kinetic resolution]\label{prop:b3:asymmetric-synthesis:dkr}
272| If the substrate enantiomers interconvert much faster than either reacts, the
273| whole racemate can be converted into one product enantiomer, with ee set by $s$:
274| $\mathrm{er} = s$.
275| \end{proposition}
276| 
277| \begin{proof}
278| Fast racemisation keeps the two substrate enantiomers in equal amounts at all
279| times. The products then form at rates in the ratio $k_{\mathrm{fast}}[\mathrm A] : k_{\mathrm{slow}}[\mathrm A] = s$, and nothing
280| stops the reaction before all the substrate, through the fast enantiomer mostly,
281| is consumed: the yield can reach 100\,\% with $\mathrm{er} = s$.
282| \end{proof}
283| 
284| \begin{method}[Choosing a strategy]\label{met:b3:asymmetric-synthesis:strategy}
285| \begin{enumerate}
286|   \item If the target's stereocentres exist in a cheap natural compound, start
287|         from the chiral pool.
288|   \item For a one-off synthesis, or to set a centre reliably next to a carbonyl
289|         group, use an auxiliary, at the cost of two extra steps.
290|   \item If the racemate is cheap and the unwanted enantiomer can be recycled or
291|         racemised, resolve it (classically, kinetically or dynamically).
292|   \item For large scale, look for an asymmetric catalyst: one stereocentre made
293|         per catalytic turnover, no stoichiometric chiral waste.
294| \end{enumerate}
295| \end{method}

297| \section{Asymmetric catalysis with metals}
298| 
299| \begin{definition}[Asymmetric catalysis]\label{def:b3:asymmetric-synthesis:asymmetric-catalysis}
300| \emph{Asymmetric catalysis}\index{asymmetric catalysis} is enantioselective
301| synthesis with a chiral catalyst used in small amount; for metal catalysts, the
302| chirality usually comes from a \emph{chiral ligand}\index{chiral ligand}.
303| \end{definition}
304| 
305| \begin{theorem}[Selectivity from energy]\label{thm:b3:asymmetric-synthesis:er-ddg}
306| If two enantiomeric products are formed through diastereomeric transition states
307| with equal pre-exponential factors, irreversibly, under kinetic control,
308| $\mathrm{er} = \exp(\Delta\Delta G^\ddagger/RT)$, where $\Delta\Delta G^\ddagger$ is the difference of their Gibbs energies of
309| activation.
310| \end{theorem}
311| 
312| \begin{proof}
313| By the Eyring equation (\cref{ch:b3:rate-theories}),
314| $k_i = (k_BT/h)\eu^{-\Delta G_i^\ddagger/RT}$; both products form from the same reactants, so at every moment
315| their rates are in the ratio $k_1/k_2 = \eu^{(\Delta G_2^\ddagger - \Delta G_1^\ddagger)/RT}$, and so are the amounts formed.
316| \end{proof}
317| 
318| At \qty{25}{\celsius} an ee of 99\,\% (er 199) needs $\Delta\Delta G^\ddagger = RT\ln 199 = \qty{13.1}{kJ/mol}$, about the energy of a
319| single hydrogen bond; at \qty{-78}{\celsius}, \qty{8.6}{kJ/mol} suffices.
320| 
321| \begin{proposition}[$C_2$-symmetric ligands]\label{prop:b3:asymmetric-synthesis:c2}
322| A $C_2$-symmetric chiral ligand halves the number of diastereomeric transition
323| states to be compared, since the two coordination sites it leaves are
324| equivalent.
325| \end{proposition}
326| 
327| \begin{proof}
328| The $C_2$ rotation of the catalyst maps one free site onto the other and leaves the
329| catalyst unchanged; any transition state at one site is therefore identical to
330| the rotated one at the other. Only the binding modes at one site (substrate face,
331| orientation) need to be compared.
332| \end{proof}
